question: The constant number of water molecules present in one formula of a single unit of salt is known as:
solution:
The correct answer is __**Water of Crystallisation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Water of crystallisation** refers to the fixed number of water molecules that are chemically bound within the crystalline structure of a compound.
 
• It is essential for maintaining the physical properties and structure of the crystal.
 
• Compounds with water of crystallisation are often called **hydrated salts**.
 
• Examples include **copper sulfate pentahydrate (CuSO₄·5H₂O)** and **gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O)**.
 
• On heating, these compounds may lose their water of crystallisation, resulting in anhydrous forms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hydrated Salts:** These are crystalline solids containing water molecules within their structure. The water molecules are known as water of crystallisation.
 
• **Anhydrous Compounds:** When hydrated salts lose their water of crystallisation upon heating, they become anhydrous. For example, heating CuSO₄·5H₂O forms anhydrous CuSO₄.
 
• **Efflorescence:** Some hydrated salts lose water of crystallisation naturally when exposed to air. This phenomenon is called efflorescence. Example: Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O).
 
• **Deliquescence:** Certain compounds absorb moisture from the air and dissolve in it to form a solution. These are called deliquescent substances, like calcium chloride (CaCl₂).
 
• **Applications:** Water of crystallisation is significant in chemical analysis, construction materials (e.g., plaster of Paris), and in maintaining the stability of certain compounds.
